title: Prepositions and idioms
blurb: Choose at, on or in for times and places, tell in from into and since from for, and use the standard preposition after verbs and adjectives.
question: An applicant's email says, “I am writing in regards to the evening program. I am interested on pediatrics, and I can start on 9 a.m. in Monday.” Which prepositions are wrong, and what should replace them?

teach.body: Formally, a preposition (at, on, in, into, for, since, with, of, to, from) links a noun or pronoun to the rest of the sentence to show time, place, direction or another relationship. An idiom is a fixed pairing that standard English expects, such as comply with or allergic to. Plain English: many of these pairings follow no logic you can work out, so the HESI A2 tests whether you know the standard one. Learn the patterns for time and place, then memorize the common pairs.

head: Preposition
Use with
Examples
rows: a clock time or exact moment
at 3 p.m., at noon, at night
on Monday, on May 4, on Thanksgiving Day
months, years, seasons, parts of the day
in May, in 2026, in the spring, in the morning
teach.caption: Smallest to largest: at a moment, on a day, in a longer period. One exception to remember: at night.
Picture it: a spot (at), a tabletop (on), a box (in).

rows.label: The chair is beside the bed.
on the unit for three days

head: Standard
Not standard
rows: depend on, insist on, focus on
aware of, prior to, abstain from
aware about, prior from, abstain of
recover from, cope with, refer to
recover of, cope to, refer at
in regard to, with regard to
teach.caption: Read the word just before the blank (the verb or adjective): the idiom belongs to that word.

teach.h: Extra prepositions, and rules that are not rules
teach.body: Cut a preposition that adds nothing: “Where is the cart at?” should be “Where is the cart?” because where already means at what place. Some old classroom rules are not errors in standard US English, so they are never the tested mistake: ending a sentence with a preposition (“Which room is she in?”) and using different than before a clause. When an option looks wrong only because of one of these, look for a real error elsewhere.

steps.label: Find the anchor word
steps.sub: The verb or adjective before the blank

teach.caption: For time and place items, ask how big the time is (moment, day, period) or what shape the place is (point, surface, enclosed).

teach.body: Nursing applicant Marcus Reed drafts: “I am writing in regards to the evening program. I am interested on pediatrics, and I can start on 9 a.m. in Monday.” In regards to is nonstandard, so he writes in regard to. The idiom is interested in. A clock time takes at, and a day takes on. Final: “I am writing in regard to the evening program. I am interested in pediatrics, and I can start at 9 a.m. on Monday.”

teach.text: Swapped time words are the HESI A2 favorite: on 3 p.m., in Monday, at May. The idiom traps are comply to, in regards to, capable to, similar with and consist in for a list of parts. Do not mark a sentence wrong just because it ends with a preposition: that is standard.

items: Time: at a clock time, on a day or date, in a month, year, season or part of the day (but at night).
Place: at a point, on a surface, in an enclosed space.
Into shows movement inside; in shows location. Since marks a starting point; for marks a length of time.
Beside means next to; besides means in addition to.
Memorize the standard idioms: comply with, consist of, capable of, responsible for, similar to, interested in, in regard to.
Cut extra prepositions (Where is it at?), but ending a sentence with a preposition is not an error.

summary: You can now choose at, on or in for times and places, and tell in from into, since from for, and beside from besides. You can also pick the standard preposition after common verbs and adjectives and cut prepositions that add nothing.

A.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The flu clinic opens ___ 8 a.m. on weekdays.”
options: at
on
in
for
A.why: A clock time takes “at”: at 8 a.m.

whyNot.1: “On” is for days and dates, not a clock time.
whyNot.2: “In” is for months, years and parts of the day, not a clock time.
whyNot.3: “For” is for a length of time (for two hours), not a starting time.

A.q: Which sentence about a patient's diet uses a standard idiom?
options: The patient must adhere with the low-salt diet.
The patient must adhere by the low-salt diet.
The patient must adhere to the low-salt diet.
The patient must adhere on the low-salt diet.

whyNot.0: “Adhere with” is nonstandard; the verb takes “to.”
whyNot.1: “By” belongs to a different idiom, “abide by”; “adhere” takes “to.”
whyNot.3: “Adhere on” is nonstandard; the verb takes “to.”

A.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “The aide placed the clean towels ___ the top shelf.”
options: in
at
on
into
A.why: A shelf is a surface, so it takes “on.”

whyNot.0: “In” is for an enclosed space; a shelf is a surface.
whyNot.1: “At” marks a point or spot, not a surface something rests on.
whyNot.3: “Into” shows movement to the inside of an enclosed space.

B.q: Which pair correctly completes the sentence? “Lena has worked at the hospital ___ 2024 and has volunteered there ___ two years.”
options: for / since
since / since
for / for
since / for
B.why: “Since” marks a starting point (since 2024); “for” marks a length of time (for two years).

whyNot.0: This reverses the pair: a year is a starting point, and two years is a length of time.
whyNot.1: “Two years” is a length of time, so it takes “for.”
whyNot.2: “2024” is a starting point, so it takes “since.”

B.q: Which sentence about a patient's surgery uses prepositions correctly?
options: The patient is aware about the risks and concerned of the cost.
The patient is aware of the risks and concerned about the cost.
The patient is aware of the risks and concerned on the cost.
The patient is aware in the risks and concerned about the cost.
B.why: The standard idioms are “aware of” and “concerned about.”

whyNot.0: Both idioms are wrong: it should be “aware of” and “concerned about.”
whyNot.2: “Concerned on” is nonstandard; the idiom is “concerned about.”
whyNot.3: “Aware in” is nonstandard; the idiom is “aware of.”

B.q: Which word in the sentence is used incorrectly? “Prior from the procedure, the patient must sign the consent form.”
options: Prior
from
must
sign
B.why: The standard idiom is “prior to,” so “from” should be “to.”

whyNot.0: “Prior” is correct; the error is the preposition that follows it.

C.q: Which sentence about a care conference uses prepositions correctly?
options: The nurse agreed to Dr. Lee and agreed with the new plan.
The nurse agreed at Dr. Lee and agreed to the new plan.
The nurse agreed with Dr. Lee and agreed of the new plan.
The nurse agreed with Dr. Lee and agreed to the new plan.
C.why: Two idioms: you agree with a person and agree to a plan or proposal.

whyNot.0: “Agreed to Dr. Lee” is nonstandard: a person takes “agree with.”
whyNot.1: “Agreed at” is nonstandard: a person takes “agree with.”
whyNot.2: “Agreed of” is nonstandard: a plan takes “agree to.”

C.q: Which sentence about the clinic contains a preposition error?
options: The trauma kit consists in gauze, tape, and two pairs of gloves.
The test results were different from what the team expected.
Which room is the new patient in?
She has been in the nursing program since last fall.
C.why: To list what something is made of, the idiom is “consists of.”

whyNot.2: Correct: ending a question with a preposition is standard English.
whyNot.3: Correct: “since” marks the starting point, last fall.

C.q: Which sentence about the clinic uses standard idioms?
options: The clinic complies to state rules and is responsible for its billing.
The clinic complies with state rules and is responsible of its billing.
The clinic complies with state rules and is responsible for its billing.
The clinic complies by state rules and is responsible for its billing.
C.why: Both idioms are standard: “comply with” and “responsible for.”

whyNot.0: “Complies to” is nonstandard; the idiom is “comply with.”
whyNot.1: “Responsible of” is nonstandard; the idiom is “responsible for.”
whyNot.3: “Complies by” mixes in “abide by”; the idiom is “comply with.”

reteach.title: Prepositions are a map and a calendar
reteach.question: Imagine giving a friend directions to a clinic appointment. Which words tell them when to come and where to stand, and why can't they be swapped?

blocks.h: Zoom in on time and place
blocks.body: Time works like zooming in on a calendar: in a month (the whole page), on a day (one square), at a time (one line in the square). Place works the same way: in a building or room (inside the walls), on a surface (the shelf, the counter), at a spot (the desk, the door). Directions such as “Come in May, on the 4th, at 9 a.m., and wait at the front desk in the main lobby” stay clear because each word fits the size of the thing.

blocks.text: Idioms are not on the map: comply with, capable of and interested in have to be memorized. When the anchor word is a verb or adjective, check the idiom table, not the zoom levels.

explain.body: At a clock time or moment, on a day or date, in a month, year, season or part of the day. The exception is at night.

test.q: Which sentence about the staff meeting uses prepositions of time correctly?
options: The meeting is in Friday at noon.
The meeting is on Friday at noon.
The meeting is on Friday in noon.
The meeting is at Friday on noon.
test.why: A day takes “on” and a clock time takes “at”: on Friday at noon.

whyNot.0: A day of the week takes “on,” not “in.”
whyNot.2: Noon is a clock time, so it takes “at.”
whyNot.3: The pair is reversed: days take “on” and clock times take “at.”

explain.body: At marks a point, on a surface and in an enclosed space. Into adds movement to the inside.

test.q: Which pair correctly completes the sentence? “The extra gloves are ___ the cabinet ___ the second shelf.”
options: in / on
on / in
at / on
in / at
test.why: A cabinet is an enclosed space (in), and a shelf is a surface (on).

whyNot.1: A shelf is a surface, so “in the second shelf” is wrong; the gloves are inside the cabinet.
whyNot.2: “At” marks a point; the gloves are inside the cabinet.
whyNot.3: A shelf is a surface and takes “on,” not “at.”

explain.body: Many verbs and adjectives take one fixed preposition. Find the anchor word just before the blank and recall its partner: comply with, cope with, depend on, allergic to, capable of, responsible for.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the sentence? “Support groups help families cope ___ a new diagnosis.”
options: to
about
for
with

whyNot.0: “Cope to” is nonstandard; the verb takes “with.”
whyNot.1: “Cope about” is nonstandard; the verb takes “with.”
whyNot.2: “Cope for” is nonstandard; the verb takes “with.”

explain.body: Cut a preposition that adds nothing (Where is it at?) and fix nonstandard set phrases (in regards to becomes in regard to). Ending a sentence with a preposition is standard and is not the error.

test.q: Which sentence about the supply room is written in standard English?
options: Where is the new thermometer at?
I am writing in regards to the supply order.
Which shelf did you put the gauze on?
The new order is similar with last month's.
test.why: Ending a question with a preposition is standard, and every other word is correct.

whyNot.0: “At” adds nothing, because “where” already means “at what place.”
whyNot.1: “In regards to” is nonstandard; the phrase is “in regard to.”
whyNot.3: The idiom is “similar to,” not “similar with.”
